Stories / Rome · Languedoc · Spain · 1584–1585

Story · Wars of Religion, 16th century

Rome, 1585: Luigi d’Este keeps Henri III informed

At the turn of 1585, while the Catholic League re-forms in France with Philip II’s money, Cardinal Luigi d’Este, who represents France in Rome, writes to Henri III’s court what he learns at the Vatican. The sensitive passages are in cipher. With the key reconstructed by Satoshi Tomokiyo, we read a long letter and a shorter passage from a volume of the Colbert collection: a rumour about Spain and Languedoc, an order from the Pope, and the warning of a French agent in Madrid.

Story by Brice Dudout · reading with Claude · key: Satoshi Tomokiyo · document: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Cinq Cents de Colbert 338 · published 14 November 2026

« m’a comandé de faire tout ce que je pourrai avec le Roy qu’il s’acomode en toute sorte avec le mareschal de Montmorenci »

“[He] ordered me to do all I can with the King so that he comes to terms in every way with Marshal de Montmorency”: the Pope to the writer, Colbert 338, p. 518 (cipher passage).

What is new, what was known

Known. Cardinal d’Este’s cipher was reconstructed by Satoshi Tomokiyo from the cardinal’s letters to Villeroy kept at the BnF (fr. 16041–16042).[1] Volume 338 of the Cinq Cents de Colbert, which he does not cite, holds other letters in this cipher; the cipher passage on p. 513 was deciphered at the time, in the margin.

What we add, to our knowledge. (1) The reading of a two-page letter entirely in cipher (pp. 517–518), with no gloss and no edition found: read (96.2%). (2) The reading of the p. 513 passage, read in part (91.5%), which agrees with the period decipherment. (3) A test of the key on a held-out portion.

The cardinal and his letters

Luigi d’Este (1538–1586), son of Duke Ercole II of Ferrara and Renée de France, was a grandson of Louis XII. A cardinal from 1561, he looked after the French king’s affairs in Rome, as his kinsman.[1] His letters to Henri III and his secretaries of state mix clear text, in French or Italian, with cipher passages in French.

Colbert 338 gathers letters and dispatches from Rome of 1584–1585.[2] p. 513 is a letter of 2 January 1585 signed by the cardinal, in clear except for a seven-line cipher block. pp. 517–518 are a letter entirely in cipher, with neither date nor signature, followed by a postscript in Italian; the cipher, the volume and the papal audience it describes link it to the cardinal. Its recipient, “vous”, is to report to the King: probably Villeroy, the usual correspondent of this cipher (hypothesis).

Rome, winter 1584–1585

The Duke of Anjou, Henri III’s brother and heir, died in June 1584; the heir is now Henri of Navarre, a Protestant. On 31 December 1584, at Joinville, the Guise and Philip II’s envoys sign a secret treaty against his succession; the League publishes its manifesto at Péronne on 31 March 1585, and Henri III gives in at the Treaty of Nemours on 7 July. In Rome, Gregory XIII is 83; he dies on 10 April 1585, and Sixtus V is elected on 24 April.[3]

The p. 513 passage, of 2 January 1585, is about that succession. According to the sieur de Longlée, Henri III’s agent at Philip II’s court, in Spain they are scheming “should the Church change its shepherd”, to strengthen their designs and weaken those of others, and “express orders” have been sent to Rome. Longlée’s dispatches have been in print since 1912; we have read one of them, in cipher, of 1590.[4] The cardinal passes on to Paris a warning from Madrid: Spain is preparing the next conclave.

Languedoc, Spain and Montmorency

The letter of pp. 517–518 turns on one man: Henri de Montmorency-Damville, Marshal of France, governor of Languedoc, a Catholic allied to the southern Protestants and in open conflict with the house of Joyeuse, the King’s favourites. The Pope, the writer says, has heard from the court of “T…” that “this duke” had received letters from the King of Spain urging him to make war on the King of France and to declare himself “protector and defender” of Montmorency. The writer hardly believes it. He thinks rather that Montmorency complained to Spain of what Marshal de Joyeuse was doing against him around the places he wanted to hold, above all Clermont-de-Lodève; that the arrival of M. de Poigny, bearing the King’s intentions, may have calmed his suspicions; and that the levy of four thousand foot raised in the State of Milan, said to be meant for the marshal, has also melted away.

The suspicion was not idle. Joan Davies showed, from the Spanish archives, Montmorency’s secret contacts with Philip II from 1582 to 1589, often through Savoy: in 1583 a servant of the marshal carried letters to Duke Charles Emmanuel hidden in his shoes; in 1585 his agent met the duke and Philip II secretly in Barcelona, during the festivities of Charles Emmanuel’s marriage to the Infanta Catalina.[5] “This duke” could therefore be the Duke of Savoy, and “the court of T…” that of Turin: a hypothesis, since the lines before p. 517 are not read.

The letter ends with an audience. As the hour drew near, the writer went to the Pope before closing his letters; they discussed Languedoc, and the Pope “ordered him to do all he can with the King” so that he “comes to terms in every way with Marshal de Montmorency” and calms the troubles. Rome is pressing Henri III to make peace with a Catholic who holds the South with the Protestants: the Pope, probably still Gregory XIII if the letter predates April 1585, fears civil war more than Montmorency’s alliance with the Huguenots. The letter is undated; it belongs to the 1584–1585 months of the volume.

The texts and their reading →

The cipher

  • Signs rather than numbers: Greek and Latin letters, Arabic figures, symbols (a Venus sign, a barred dumbbell), with several signs for the same letter.
  • Code words for the King, the Pope, Monsieur, Spain (the sign “y”, which the decipherer of p. 513 renders “Espaigne”).
  • Nulls, to mislead the reader.

The key is Satoshi Tomokiyo’s, with our names for the shapes and a few values added on the pages of the volume that were already glossed.

How we read it

  1. A first, partial test. On 5 November 2026, p. 523 of the same volume, held out, scored 0.457 against 0.078 for the best control: below the bar then set (0.60). Result declared “partial”.
  2. A bar revised before the measurement. For the next key, we found that the period decipherments themselves score only 0.50 to 0.73 on this measure: a bar of 0.60 would reject correct readings. The protocol, hashed before the block to be measured was transcribed, therefore set the bar at 0.45 (and at least 0.30 above the best control), with this justification in figures. We declare it: the choice was made before the measurement, not after.
  3. A single measurement. Held-out block: p. 517, lines 4 to 29 (979 signs), transcribed in two passes and frozen. Score 0.509 against at best 0.067 for 200 control keys: key validated.
  4. Reading for sense, word by word. p. 518 was transcribed by two readers, the second blind; so was p. 513, whose margin, carrying the period decipherment, was looked at only after our transcription was frozen.
  5. Brice Dudout’s blind re-reading. A sheet of six doubtful shapes, with two control questions and no reading visible, asked him to choose the shape he saw; the integration rules were hashed beforehand. Both controls were passed. The sign “6” at the start of p. 518 is an o: one must read “pour estre de la nature qu’elles sont”, and p. 518 rises from 94.4% to 95.4%.

What remains uncertain

  • Letter pp. 517–518: read. 339 cipher words, 326 certain or probable, i.e. 96.2%; p. 517 alone reaches 96.5%, p. 518 alone 95.4%. The code word “Spain” is restored by sense there and not counted. In Daniel Bourdeau’s repository, the integration notes that counting certain words only, p. 517 would fall to 87.0%.
  • p. 513: read in part (43 words of 47, 91.5%), and too short for a measurement. Its text was already known from the marginal gloss.
  • Values that are only probable. The new shapes of pp. 517–518 could not be tested, for lack of a fresh 300-sign portion.
  • Date and writer. The letter pp. 517–518 is neither dated nor signed; its attribution to the cardinal and its date (1584–1585) rest on the cipher and the volume.
  • The context (Joyeuse, Poigny, the Milan levy, the identity of “this duke”) is checked only on general works and on J. Davies’ article; specialised studies of Montmorency-Damville were not consulted.
  • No image. The volume can be seen on Gallica.
